claim: Parabrachial CGRP neurons receive diverse threat-related signals.
source: Parabrachial CGRP neurons receive diverse threat-related signals and contribute to multiple phases of adaptive threat responses in mice
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of CGRPPBN neurons, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Inactivation of CGRPPBN neurons attenuates unconditioned behavioral responses to somatic pain.
source: with their inactivation attenuating both unconditioned behavioral responses to somatic pain and fear-memory formation
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Han et al., 2015) mentioned in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Inactivation of CGRPPBN neurons attenuates fear-memory formation.
source: with their inactivation attenuating both unconditioned behavioral responses to somatic pain and fear-memory formation
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Han et al., 2015).

claim: CGRPPBN neurons respond broadly to multi-modal threats.
source: Because CGRPPBN neurons respond broadly to multi-modal threats, it remains unknown how these distinct adaptive processes are individually engaged.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Campos et al., 2018) in the introduction.

claim: Three partially separable subsets of CGRPPBN neurons broadly collateralize to their respective downstream partners.
source: We show that while three partially separable subsets of CGRPPBN neurons broadly collateralize to their respective downstream partners, individual projections accomplish distinct functions
evidence: This is supported by the collateralization tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hypothalamic and extended amygdalar projections from CGRPPBN neurons elicit unconditioned threat responses including autonomic arousal, anxiety, and freezing behavior.
source: hypothalamic and extended amygdalar projections elicit assorted unconditioned threat responses including autonomic arousal, anxiety, and freezing behavior
evidence: This is supported by terminal photostimulation experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Thalamic and basal forebrain projections from CGRPPBN neurons generate freezing behavior.
source: while thalamic and basal forebrain projections generate freezing behavior and, unexpectedly, contribute to associative fear learning
evidence: This is supported by terminal photostimulation experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Thalamic and basal forebrain projections from CGRPPBN neurons contribute to associative fear learning.
source: while thalamic and basal forebrain projections generate freezing behavior and, unexpectedly, contribute to associative fear learning
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic conditioning and photoinhibition experiments shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Unconditioned responses generated by individual CGRPPBN projections are complementary.
source: Moreover, the unconditioned responses generated by individual projections are complementary, with simultaneous activation of multiple sites driving profound freezing behavior and bradycardia that are not elicited by any individual projection.
evidence: This is supported by multi-fiber stimulation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Simultaneous activation of multiple CGRPPBN projection sites drives profound freezing behavior not elicited by any individual projection.
source: with simultaneous activation of multiple sites driving profound freezing behavior and bradycardia that are not elicited by any individual projection
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing that combined VPMpc and cCeA stimulation produces robust freezing.

claim: Simultaneous activation of multiple CGRPPBN projection sites drives bradycardia not elicited by any individual projection.
source: with simultaneous activation of multiple sites driving profound freezing behavior and bradycardia that are not elicited by any individual projection
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6G showing bradycardia from combined VPMpc and cCeA stimulation.

claim: Imminent threats such as somatic pain rapidly shape ongoing behavior in rodents.
source: Imminent threats such as somatic pain rapidly shape ongoing behavior and alter physiology to prioritize immediate threat remediation (LeDoux, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to LeDoux, 2000.

claim: Rodent threat responses can include bouts of active escape or freezing behavior.
source: This cascade of activity, which in rodents can include bouts of active escape or freezing behavior (Blanchard and Blanchard, 1969; Fanselow, 1982; Roelofs, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Blanchard and Blanchard, 1969; Fanselow, 1982; Roelofs, 2017).

claim: Rodent threat responses include autonomic changes with enhanced sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow.
source: and autonomic changes, including both enhanced sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow (Fitzgerald and Teyler, 1970; Iwata and LeDoux, 1988)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Fitzgerald and Teyler, 1970; Iwata and LeDoux, 1988).

claim: A later phase of threat response includes enhanced arousal, wariness and anxiety.
source: A later phase of threat response includes enhanced arousal, wariness and anxiety (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Aversive threat signals are transmitted to forebrain nuclei that receive convergent information about ongoing environmental stimuli to form associations.
source: In tandem to these innate adaptive responses, the aversive threat signal is transmitted to forebrain nuclei that receive convergent information about ongoing environmental stimuli, and associations are formed allowing prediction of future threats based on environmental information (Blair et al., 2001; Bolles and Collier, 1976; LeDoux, 2000; Maren, 2001; Romanski et al., 1993; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Blair et al., 2001; Bolles and Collier, 1976; LeDoux, 2000; Maren, 2001; Romanski et al., 1993; Tovote et al., 2015).

claim: Re-exposure to pain-predictive cues reactivates nuclei storing associative memory and triggers responses previously characteristic of the unconditioned response.
source: Upon re-exposure to pain-predictive cues (e.g. an auditory conditioning stimulus (CS)), nuclei storing the associative memory are reactivated and through downstream partners trigger responses previously hallmarks of the unconditioned response (e.g. freezing behavior and autonomic arousal) (Goosens and Maren, 2001; Iwata and LeDoux, 1988; Maren, 2001; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Goosens and Maren, 2001; Iwata and LeDoux, 1988; Maren, 2001; Tovote et al., 2015).

claim: The parabrachial nucleus is located at the junction of the midbrain and pons.
source: The parabrachial nucleus (PBN), located at the junction of the midbrain and pons, is implicated in relaying aversive threat information to the forebrain (Bernard and Besson, 1988; Chiang et al., 2019; Gauriau and Bernard, 2002).
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact.

claim: The parabrachial nucleus is implicated in relaying aversive threat information to the forebrain.
source: The parabrachial nucleus (PBN), located at the junction of the midbrain and pons, is implicated in relaying aversive threat information to the forebrain (Bernard and Besson, 1988; Chiang et al., 2019; Gauriau and Bernard, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Bernard and Besson, 1988; Chiang et al., 2019; Gauriau and Bernard, 2002).

claim: CGRP neurons reside in the external lateral PBN.
source: A recently identified population of neurons expressing calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP, encoded by the Calca gene) resides in the external lateral PBN
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data in the manuscript and prior literature.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons are robustly activated by threats of diverse origin.
source: A recently identified population of neurons expressing calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP, encoded by the Calca gene) resides in the external lateral PBN and is robustly activated by threats of diverse origin (Campos et al., 2017; Campos et al., 2018; Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018), including somatic pain (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Campos et al., 2017; Campos et al., 2018; Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018).

claim: CGRPPBN neurons are robustly activated by somatic pain.
source: and is robustly activated by threats of diverse origin (Campos et al., 2017; Campos et al., 2018; Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018), including somatic pain (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Han et al., 2015.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons contribute to affective and behavioral responses to pain.
source: In addition to contributing to affective and behavioral responses to pain, CGRPPBN neurons are necessary for associative fear learning (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Han et al., 2015.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons are necessary for associative fear learning.
source: In addition to contributing to affective and behavioral responses to pain, CGRPPBN neurons are necessary for associative fear learning (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Han et al., 2015.

claim: Repeated high-frequency (30 Hz) activation of CGRPPBN neurons induced profound freezing behavior.
source: Repeated high-frequency (30 Hz) activation of CGRPPBN neurons induced profound freezing behavior (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C and Figure 1—video 1), as indicated by rigid, uninterrupted immobility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pairing photostimulation of CGRPPBN neurons with an auditory CS rapidly induced conditioned freezing responses to the CS.
source: In addition to eliciting robust freezing behavior, we confirmed that pairing photostimulation with an auditory CS rapidly induced conditioned freezing responses to the CS (Figure 1C; Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Han et al., 2015.

claim: Modest activation (15 Hz) of CGRPPBN neurons resulted in moderate tachycardia.
source: Interestingly, while modest activation (15 Hz, subthreshold for eliciting freezing behavior) resulted in moderate tachycardia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: High-frequency activation (30 Hz) of CGRPPBN neurons led to profound bradycardia.
source: high-frequency activation (30 Hz) led to profound bradycardia and decreased respiration followed by dramatic post-stimulation rebound tachycardia and mild hyperventilation (Figure 1E–F, respiration measured in plethysmography chamber)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: High-frequency activation (30 Hz) of CGRPPBN neurons led to decreased respiration.
source: high-frequency activation (30 Hz) led to profound bradycardia and decreased respiration followed by dramatic post-stimulation rebound tachycardia and mild hyperventilation (Figure 1E–F, respiration measured in plethysmography chamber)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: High-frequency activation (30 Hz) of CGRPPBN neurons produced vasoconstriction.
source: it also produced vasoconstriction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H; Vianna and Carrive, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and citation to Vianna and Carrive, 2005.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons are capable of exerting opposing effects on autonomic physiology depending on their activation frequency.
source: Hence, CGRPPBN neurons are capable of exerting opposing effects on autonomic physiology depending on their activation frequency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 15 Hz stimulation causes tachycardia while 30 Hz causes bradycardia.

claim: Freezing behavior is rapidly initiated with a median latency of 0.42 s during 30 Hz photostimulation of CGRPPBN neurons.
source: Comparing the latencies of somatic vs autonomic responses to 30 Hz photostimulation, we found that freezing behavior is rapidly initiated (median 0.42 s), while bradycardia takes longer to develop (median 22.15 s, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Bradycardia takes longer to develop (median 22.15 s) during 30 Hz photostimulation of CGRPPBN neurons.
source: Comparing the latencies of somatic vs autonomic responses to 30 Hz photostimulation, we found that freezing behavior is rapidly initiated (median 0.42 s), while bradycardia takes longer to develop (median 22.15 s, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Freezing behavior does not emerge simply as a consequence of adverse autonomic effects.
source: suggesting that freezing behavior does not emerge simply as a consequence of adverse autonomic effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that freezing occurs much faster than bradycardia.

claim: Activation of CGRPPBN neurons during elevated-plus-maze test attenuated open-arm exploration consistent with an anxiogenic effect.
source: To test whether CGRPPBN neurons can also elicit behavioral alterations associated with late-phase responses to threat exposure, we subjected mice to an elevated-plus-maze test (Martin, 1961; Pellow et al., 1985) while activating CGRPPBN neurons; this treatment attenuated open-arm exploration consistent with an anxiogenic effect (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and citations (Martin, 1961; Pellow et al., 1985).

claim: CGRPPBN neurons have major projections to the central amygdala (~40%, primarily targeting the capsular sub-nucleus).
source: Comparing individual targets to cumulative projection intensity, we found major projections to the central amygdala (CeA,~40%, primarily targeting the capsular sub-nucleus)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons have major projections to the substantia innominata (~20%).
source: substantia innominata (SI,~20%)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons have major projections to the oval sub-nucleus of the bed nucleus of stria terminalis (~15%).
source: and oval sub-nucleus of the bed nucleus of stria terminalis (ovBNST,~15%)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons have weaker projections to the parasubthalamic nucleus and thalamus (~10% each).
source: with weaker projections to the parasubthalamic nucleus, thalamus and visceral insular cortex; PSTN and VPMpc,~10% each
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons have weaker projections to the visceral insular cortex (~5%).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons target the contralateral hemisphere for all of their downstream partners except the IC.
source: With the exception of the IC, CGRPPBN neurons also target the contralateral hemisphere for all of their downstream partners, markedly to the contralateral PSTN and VPMpc, with ~75% and 50% of the ipsilateral projection intensity, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: All major downstream targets of CGRPPBN neurons receive reliable excitatory input.
source: Interestingly, we found that while all the major downstream targets were recipients of reliable excitatory input from CGRPPBN neurons (Figure 1J, IC not tested)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The VPMpc exhibited significantly greater excitation from CGRPPBN terminal activation than any other recording site.
source: the VPMpc, while not receiving the strongest input based on fiber density, exhibited significantly greater excitation from terminal activation than any other recording site (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: CeA-projecting CGRPPBN neurons contributed substantially to PSTN, SI, VPMpc and ovBNST projections, but not IC.
source: This analysis revealed that CeA-projectors contributed substantially to PSTN, SI, VPMpc and ovBNST projections, but not IC.
evidence: This is supported by collateralization tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VPMpc-projecting CGRPPBN neurons contributed substantially to the SI and IC.
source: VPMpc-projectors, interestingly, while also projecting to the CeA, contributed more substantially to the SI and IC
evidence: This is supported by collateralization tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PSTN-projecting CGRPPBN neurons had limited secondary output to the CeA and SI.
source: while PSTN-projectors had limited secondary output to the CeA and SI
evidence: This is supported by collateralization tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ovBNST-projecting CGRPPBN neurons had only a weak secondary projection to the CeA.
source: and ovBNST-projectors had only a weak secondary projection to the CeA (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by collateralization tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Neurons projecting to the CeA made up the largest proportion of CGRPPBN neurons residing within the external lateral PBN.
source: Quantifying the number and location of the different projecting subpopulations within the PBN revealed that neurons projecting to the CeA made up the largest proportion of CGRPPBN neurons residing within the external lateral PBN
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Neurons projecting to VPMpc accounted for most of the CGRPPBN neurons residing in the medial and waist regions.
source: while neurons projecting to VPMpc accounted for most of the CGRPPBN neurons residing in the medial and waist regions
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Neurons projecting to ovBNST were restricted to the external lateral PBN.
source: neurons projecting to ovBNST, the smallest group, were restricted to the external lateral PBN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Regardless of the downstream target used to drive expression, the CeA was the primary downstream partner in terms of projection intensity.
source: Comparing projection distributions for the Target + or Target - expression conditions, we found that regardless of the downstream target used to drive expression, the CeA was the primary downstream partner in terms of projection intensity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: VPMpc-projecting CGRPPBN neurons had the greatest tendency to collateralize.
source: Looking at the distribution of these coefficients across secondary downstream partners for each target site, we found that VPMpc projectors had the greatest tendency to collateralize
evidence: This is supported by collateralization coefficient analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ovBNST-projecting CGRPPBN neurons collateralized primarily to the CeA.
source: while ovBNST projectors collateralized primarily to the CeA (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by collateralization coefficient analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There is extensive collateralization by CGRPPBN neurons with no one-to-one projections.
source: In summary, there is extensive collateralization by CGRPPBN neurons with no one-to-one projections
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collateralization tracing experiments.

claim: CGRPPBN neurons tend to distribute their projections among large groups of downstream targets, composing a one-to-many distributed projection arrangement.
source: rather, CGRPPBN neurons tend to distribute their projections among large groups of downstream targets, composing a one-to-many distributed projection arrangement (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collateralization tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Photostimulating terminals in the VPMpc led to reliable initiation of freezing behavior (~40% time-spent freezing).
source: Only photostimulating terminals in the VPMpc or PSTN led to reliable initiation of freezing behavior (Figure 3A–B,~40% time-spent freezing)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Photostimulating terminals in the PSTN led to reliable initiation of freezing behavior (~40% time-spent freezing).
source: Only photostimulating terminals in the VPMpc or PSTN led to reliable initiation of freezing behavior (Figure 3A–B,~40% time-spent freezing)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Photostimulating terminals in the cCeA had subtle effects on freezing behavior (~25% time-spent freezing).
source: while photostimulating the caudal CeA (cCeA), SI, or ovBNST had more subtle effects (~25% time-spent freezing, Figure 3C–F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Photostimulating terminals in the SI had subtle effects on freezing behavior (~25% time-spent freezing).
source: while photostimulating the caudal CeA (cCeA), SI, or ovBNST had more subtle effects (~25% time-spent freezing, Figure 3C–F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Photostimulating terminals in the ovBNST had subtle effects on freezing behavior (~25% time-spent freezing).
source: while photostimulating the caudal CeA (cCeA), SI, or ovBNST had more subtle effects (~25% time-spent freezing, Figure 3C–F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Stimulating the rCeA led to a non-significant increase in locomotion.
source: and stimulating the rostral CeA (rCeA) actually led to a non-significant increase in locomotion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Activating no individual projection was able to match CGRPPBN cell-body activation in generating robust freezing behavior.
source: Notably, activating no individual projection was able to match CGRPPBN cell-body activation in generating robust freezing behavior (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: Photostimulation led to short-latency freezing bout initiation (<5 s after stimulation onset) for most terminal stimulation groups except the rCeA.
source: We found that photostimulation led to short-latency freezing bout initiation (<5 s after stimulation onset) for most terminal stimulation groups except the rCeA, which instead elicited short-latency freezing bouts after stimulation offset (~2.4 s) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: rCeA terminal stimulation elicited short-latency freezing bouts after stimulation offset (~2.4 s).
source: which instead elicited short-latency freezing bouts after stimulation offset (~2.4 s) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: Stimulation of most CGRPPBN neuron projections simultaneously elicits a direct effect on freezing behavior while also generating aversive properties that promote transient contextual freezing.
source: When taken together with the observation that freezing behavior occurs with greater frequency during the stimulation epoch than post-stimulation epoch for all fiber-placement groups except those in the CeA and ovBNST (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), these findings suggest that stimulation of most CGRPPBN neuron projections simultaneously elicits a direct effect on freezing behavior while also generating aversive properties that promote transient contextual freezing.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal pattern of freezing responses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: In the case of the rCeA, the direct effect on freezing is absent, while the contextual memory effects on freezing are the primary effect.
source: Interestingly, in the case of the rCeA, the direct effect on freezing is absent, while the contextual memory effects on freezing are instead the primary effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal pattern of freezing responses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Activating terminals in the PSTN caused mild tachycardia.
source: Photostimulating terminals in the PSTN (n = 6,5) elicited freezing behavior, (H) caused mild tachycardia
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Activating terminals in the PSTN caused vasoconstriction.
source: but (T) caused vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3T.

claim: Activating terminals in the rCeA elicited robust tachycardia.
source: Photostimulating terminals in the rCeA (n = 6,5) had no effect on freezing behavior (J) elicited robust tachycardia
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Activating terminals in the rCeA caused hyperventilation.
source: (P) hyperventilation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3P.

claim: Activating terminals in the rCeA caused vasoconstriction.
source: and (V) vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3V.

claim: Activating terminals in the SI caused tachycardia.
source: Photostimulating terminals in the SI (n = 8,6) increased freezing behavior, (K) caused tachycardia
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Activating terminals in the SI caused vasoconstriction.
source: and (W) caused vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3W.

claim: Activating terminals in the ovBNST caused tachycardia.
source: Photostimulating terminals in the ovBNST (n = 9,5) increased freezing behavior, (L) caused tachycardia
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Activating terminals in the ovBNST caused hyperventilation.
source: and (R) hyperventilation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3R.

claim: Photostimulation of terminals in each downstream target did not generate antidromic activation of CGRPPBN cell bodies sufficiently to induce Fos expression in the PBN.
source: In support of this conclusion, we observed that photostimulation of terminals in each downstream target did not generate antidromic activation of CGRPPBN cell bodies sufficiently to induce Fos expression in the PBN (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Only photostimulation of terminals in the ovBNST significantly reduced open-arm exploration, consistent with an anxiogenic effect.
source: Only photostimulation of terminals in the ovBNST significantly reduced open-arm exploration, consistent with an anxiogenic effect
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: Photostimulating terminals in the rCeA paradoxically increased open-arm exploration.
source: while photostimulating terminals in the rCeA paradoxically increased open-arm exploration (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: Mice with photostimulation of CGRPPBN somata robustly avoided photostimulation in RTPP assay.
source: Mice with photostimulation of either CGRPPBN somata or their terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, rCeA, or SI robustly avoided photostimulation (Figure 4E–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–K)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mice with photostimulation of terminals in the VPMpc robustly avoided photostimulation in RTPP assay.
source: Mice with photostimulation of either CGRPPBN somata or their terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, rCeA, or SI robustly avoided photostimulation (Figure 4E–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–K)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mice with photostimulation of terminals in the PSTN robustly avoided photostimulation in RTPP assay.
source: Mice with photostimulation of either CGRPPBN somata or their terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, rCeA, or SI robustly avoided photostimulation (Figure 4E–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–K)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Mice with photostimulation of terminals in the rCeA robustly avoided photostimulation in RTPP assay.
source: Mice with photostimulation of either CGRPPBN somata or their terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, rCeA, or SI robustly avoided photostimulation (Figure 4E–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–K)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Mice with photostimulation of terminals in the SI robustly avoided photostimulation in RTPP assay.
source: Mice with photostimulation of either CGRPPBN somata or their terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, rCeA, or SI robustly avoided photostimulation (Figure 4E–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–K)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Mice with photostimulation of terminals in the cCeA had no place preference relative to control animals.
source: whereas mice with photostimulation of terminals in the cCeA or ovBNST had no preference relative to control animals, which spent equal time in the three compartments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Mice with photostimulation of terminals in the ovBNST had no place preference relative to control animals.
source: whereas mice with photostimulation of terminals in the cCeA or ovBNST had no preference relative to control animals, which spent equal time in the three compartments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Photostimulation of CGRPPBN-neuron terminals in the VPMpc resulted in significant freezing to the auditory CS after 6 CS-US pairings.
source: Photostimulation of CGRPPBN-neuron terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, or SI resulted in significant freezing to the auditory CS after 6 CS-US pairings (Figure 5B–G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Photostimulation of CGRPPBN-neuron terminals in the PSTN resulted in significant freezing to the auditory CS after 6 CS-US pairings.
source: Photostimulation of CGRPPBN-neuron terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, or SI resulted in significant freezing to the auditory CS after 6 CS-US pairings (Figure 5B–G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Photostimulation of CGRPPBN-neuron terminals in the SI resulted in significant freezing to the auditory CS after 6 CS-US pairings.
source: Photostimulation of CGRPPBN-neuron terminals in the VPMpc, PSTN, or SI resulted in significant freezing to the auditory CS after 6 CS-US pairings (Figure 5B–G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Only activation of terminals in the VPMpc or SI generated a significant association as indicated by area under the curve exceeding that of control animals.
source: with only activation of terminals in the VPMpc or SI generating a significant association as indicated by area under the curve exceeding that of control animals (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Activation of terminals in the VPMpc or SI generated robust conditioned freezing to the CS in a novel context 24 hr following conditioning.
source: and robust conditioned freezing to the CS in a novel context 24 hr following conditioning (Figure 5B–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5F.

claim: The association formed by photostimulation of CGRPPBN neuron terminals in either the SI or VPMpc is weaker than that driven by photostimulating CGRPPBN neuron cell bodies.
source: While photostimulation of CGRPPBN neuron terminals in either the SI or VPMpc was sufficient to drive associative fear learning, the association formed is weaker than that driven by photostimulating CGRPPBN neuron cell bodies (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Combining photostimulation of terminals in the VPMpc and SI led to rapid entrainment of freezing behavior to an auditory CS.
source: Combining photostimulation of terminals in the VPMpc and SI (10 mW each) led to rapid entrainment of freezing behavior to an auditory CS
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Simultaneous activation of terminals in the VPMpc and cCeA elicited robust freezing behavior exceeding that produced individually.
source: while simultaneous activation of terminals in the VPMpc and cCeA elicited robust freezing behavior exceeding that produced individually (VPMpc 37.1 ± 2.3% freezing; cCeA 23.2 ± 0.5; Combined 68.9 ± 3.6 (mean ± sem), Figure 6B and E–F; Figure 6—video 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–F.

claim: Simultaneous photostimulation of terminals in the cCeA and VPMpc robustly elicited bradycardia.
source: We also tested whether simultaneous photostimulation of terminals in the cCeA and VPMpc would affect autonomic physiology by measuring heart rate using a pulse oximeter. While activating neither projection alone affected heart rate (Figure 3), simultaneous photostimulation robustly elicited bradycardia
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Bradycardia consistently took longer to develop than freezing responses during simultaneous photostimulation of terminals in the cCeA and VPMpc.
source: which consistently took longer to develop than freezing responses (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Selective inhibition of CGRPPBN neurons during the foot shock significantly attenuated conditioned responses during training.
